conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’ve been admitted because of a gastrointestinal bleed. Can you tell me about your symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, doc. I’ve had blood in my stool for about four days now. Not black or tarry, just mixed in. I’ve been feeling weak, dizzy, and really tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you had dialysis the day before coming in. Your hematocrit dropped from 33.9 to 22.6, which is significant. We gave you one unit of blood in the ER. How’s your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little short, especially when I lie down. I started coughing yesterday too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in the lungs—moderate pulmonary edema. Given your heart and kidney history, this is likely from fluid overload. We’ll monitor that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so puffy? My legs are okay, but I just feel heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s consistent. We’ll adjust your medications and plan for dialysis tomorrow to help remove excess fluid. But first, we need to find the source of the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bleeds before—stomach and intestines. But not since I stopped blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. You’re not on Coumadin due to past bleeds. We’ll avoid anything that could worsen bleeding. We’re starting you on IV fluids and a proton pump inhibitor to reduce stomach acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been itching like crazy since I got here. Is that from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have prurigo nodularis, which we see in some dialysis patients. We’ll continue your Aquaphor, Sarna, and Benadryl as needed. It’s not from new meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do an upper endoscopy tomorrow to look for the bleed source. You’ll be sedated, and we’ll check your esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be asleep during the procedure. You’ll wake up shortly after. It’s very safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re getting you ready for your endoscopy. Any questions before we go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m ready. Just want to know what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The endoscopy showed severe esophagitis—significant inflammation in your esophagus. That’s likely where the bleeding came from. There was also mild duodenitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Esophagitis? Like acid reflux?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You also have a small hiatal hernia, which can make reflux worse. We’re switching you to high-dose IV pantoprazole to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on omeprazole. Is this stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re giving it twice daily. You’ll go home on 40 mg twice a day. Also, no NSAIDs—no ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin except your 81 mg heart dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my heart rate? It’s been racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After the procedure, you were in rapid atrial fibrillation. We gave IV diltiazem and increased your oral dose to 60 mg four times a day. It’s under control now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on diltiazem already. Is that safe with my heart failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted it cautiously. It helps control your rate. We held your usual long-acting dose initially but are now on a short-acting form you take four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding lisinopril for now due to the bleed and low hemoglobin. Diltiazem will help with both rate and pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had two more units of blood. How’s my count now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had three total. Your hemoglobin is stabilizing. We’ll check it again tomorrow. You’re not actively bleeding now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have hemodialysis this afternoon. It will help clear fluid and toxins. We’ll monitor your heart during it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs show your potassium dropped to 3.0 and magnesium to 1.9. You had two brief episodes of NSVT—non-sustained ventricular tachycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I felt a flutter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. We’ve given potassium and magnesium supplements. No further episodes since. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My belly’s been hurting—left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray. No perforation or obstruction. There’s some increased lung opacities on the left, likely from the edema. Pain may be from that or bowel irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No colonoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. Since the upper endoscopy found a likely source and you’re not bleeding now, we’ll do outpatient colonoscopy and repeat EGD in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your CMV and HSV antibodies. CMV IgG is positive, IgM negative—means past exposure, not active infection. HSV IgG positive, but no signs of outbreak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. CMV can reactivate if immunity drops, but you’re stable. No treatment needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My graft site hurts. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. The renal team thinks it could be steal syndrome. They recommend seeing transplant surgery as an outpatient to evaluate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Am I getting better overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your breathing is better, no active bleeding, heart rhythm stable. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all stays well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable. We’re discharging you today. You’ll go home on high-dose omeprazole, continue all other meds except lisinopril for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your PCP, GI for repeat endoscopy and colonoscopy, and transplant surgery for your graft pain. Get a CBC drawn next week and fax it to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh daily. Call if you gain more than three pounds in a day. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep up with your appointments.
